name: Murvah Iqbal

education.degree: BA Development Economics and International Development
education.notes: Awarded North West Student of the Year by Young Enterprise during/around this period. 2016 university trip to Silicon Valley was the load-bearing event — she met future co-founder Mathias Krieger there.

keyDecisions: Committed to elite youth football through teens — long-cycle competitive discipline before any business work.
lessons: Sport at a serious level teaches tolerance for repeated public failure that translates directly to fundraising rejection.
Captaining a team in your teens is a cheap leadership reps — most graduate hires get their first real reps at 25+.
careerSteps.notes: Working-class Manchester upbringing; captain of academy side.

keyDecisions: Took on a real brand-marketing role inside a family-adjacent business from age 14 — operating reps before any classroom theory.
Did this in parallel with elite sport and school — high-density teenage years, not balanced ones.
lessons: Early operating reps inside a small, profitable family business beat any classroom MBA content for pattern recognition.
Parallel pursuits in your teens (sport + business + school) train context-switching, which is the actual founder skill.
careerSteps.notes: Title 'Head of Brand Marketing' is self-described and unusually senior for the age; treat as substantive entrepreneurial exposure rather than a formal executive role.

keyDecisions: Chose development economics rather than business/CS — kept a systems-and-incentives lens.
Signed up for the 2016 university trip to Silicon Valley — the single highest-leverage line item in the degree.
Used that trip to meet future co-founder Mathias Krieger — converted a tourist itinerary into a co-founder relationship.
lessons: Optional university travel programmes can be the highest-leverage line item in a degree — that one trip set the co-founder relationship that built two companies.
Treat university not as the curriculum but as the connection-density it gives you access to.

keyDecisions: Started with the adjacent, simpler problem (advertising on delivery vans) rather than going straight at logistics — bought herself a way in without needing huge capital.
Wound it down cleanly when the model didn't work, instead of forcing a heroic pivot.
lessons: A small failed/wound-down first venture in an adjacent niche can be the cheapest way to acquire the real insight — Vanvas got Iqbal and Krieger inside the delivery industry before HIVED.
Don't romanticise the pivot — Vanvas wasn't a heroic pivot, it was a wind-down with one good takeaway, which is fine.
First ventures are tuition, not identity.
careerSteps.notes: Short-lived. Surfaced inefficiencies in the parcel-delivery industry that became the HIVED thesis.

keyDecisions: Built all-electric from day one rather than retrofitting — turned regulation (London ULEZ, retailer net-zero targets) into a moat instead of a cost.
Targeted big retail brands (ASOS, Zara, Nespresso) early rather than the SME long-tail — bet the company on enterprise sales from week one.
Cold-outreached VCs without warm intros — replaced the network she didn't have with a sharper wedge.
Chose a 'schlep' market (logistics: capex-heavy, regulated, operationally brutal) that warm-network founders systematically avoid.
lessons: If you have no warm-intro VC network, replace it with extreme specificity in cold outreach plus a defensible wedge (electric-only fleet) that the warm-intro founders can't match.
Pick a market where your customer's incentives (corporate ESG targets, ULEZ compliance) compound your sales pitch over time — regulation as a tailwind, not an obstacle.
Logistics is a 'schlep' market in PG's sense — high-capex, regulated, operationally brutal — which is exactly why it's underserved by the typical first-time founder.
Non-traditional founder background + sharp wedge can beat traditional background + generic wedge in late-stage fundraising.
careerSteps.notes: Self-reports starting HIVED 'when I was 24' in Founders Everywhere interview — consistent with 2021 founding given 1996 birth year. Reported 22% MoM growth since inception. Raised ~$12.4M Series A (2023) and a ~$42M Series B (reported 2024). Forbes 30 Under 30 (2023). Co-founder Mathias Krieger met on the 2016 King's College Silicon Valley trip.

outcomes.currentStatus: Co-founder & CEO of HIVED, scaling zero-emission last-mile parcel delivery across the UK. No exit; net worth is paper-only equity.

lessons.lesson: First venture (van advertising) surfaced the real logistics-pain insight that became HIVED — adjacent-business probe rather than heroic pivot.
Cold-outreach VC fundraising works if the wedge is sharp enough — warm intros are nice-to-have, not required.
Use regulation (ULEZ, corporate net-zero pledges) as a tailwind, not an obstacle.
Optional university travel programmes can be the highest-leverage line item in a degree — one Silicon Valley trip set the co-founder relationship.
